The '''2022 Havering London Borough Council election''' was held on 5 May 2022 to elect all 55 members of [[Havering London Borough Council]]. The elections took place alongside [[2022 London local elections|local elections in the other London boroughs]] and [[2022 United Kingdom local elections|elections to local authorities across the United Kingdom]].

In the [[2018 Havering London Borough Council election|previous election in 2018]], the council remained under [[no overall control]]. The [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]] were the largest party, winning 25 out of the 55 seats with the [[Havering Residents Association]] forming the principal opposition with 17 of the remaining seats.

The 2022 election took place under new election boundaries, which increased the number of councillors to 55. The Conservatives remained the largest party and the council remained under no overall control. After weeks of negotiations, Conservative leader Damian White was replaced by HRA leader Ray Morgon on 25 May as Leader of the Council in a coalition with Labour.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Newsdesk |date=2022-05-27 |title=Labour team up with Havering Residents Association to elect independent council leader |url=https://www.nelondoner.co.uk/news/27052022-labour-team-up-with-havering-residents-association-to-elect-independent-council-leader |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=North East Londoner |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Background ==

=== History ===
[[File:Havering London UK local election 2018 map.svg|thumb|Result of the 2018 borough election]]
The thirty-two [[London boroughs]] were established in 1965 by the [[London Government Act 1963]]. They are the principal authorities in Greater London and have responsibilities including education, housing, planning, highways, social services, libraries, recreation, waste, environmental health and revenue collection. Some of the powers are shared with the [[Greater London Authority]], which also manages passenger transport, police and fire.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The essential guide to London local government {{!}} London Councils|url=https://www.londoncouncils.gov.uk/who-runs-london/essential-guide-london-local-government|access-date=2021-10-10|website=www.londoncouncils.gov.uk}}</ref>

Since its formation, Havering has most often been under [[no overall control]] with no single political party holding a majority of its seats. It has also been controlled by the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] for nineteen years and by the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] for three years. Local elections have seen Conservative, Labour and [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrat]] councillors returned, with the last Liberal Democrat councillor having been elected in 2006. The [[2006 Havering London Borough Council election|2006 election]] also saw a [[British National Party]] candidate elected, and the [[2014 Havering London Borough Council election|2014 election]] resulted in the election of a [[UK Independence Party]] candidate. The authority also has a long history of independent and [[residents' association]] candidates winning election, including the [[Havering Residents Association]] (HRA).

In the [[2018 Havering London Borough Council election|most recent elections in 2018]], the Conservatives won 25 seats with 37.1%; the HRA won 17 seats with the one elected [[Harold Hill Independent Party]] winning one councillor who joined the HRA's group; and the Labour Party and independent residents won five seats each. The only councillor elected as an independent, Michael Deon-Burton for South Hornchurch, joined the Conservative group later in May 2021 and was named as deputy mayor of the council.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Clemenson|first=Matthew|date=2018-05-31|title=Havering councillor who joined Conservatives after being elected as independent speaks out after wave of abuse|url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/havering-councillor-speaks-out-after-joining-tories-led-to-personal-3169706|access-date=2021-10-18|website=Romford Recorder|language=en-UK}}</ref> The result was the only hung council in Greater London.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Grafton-Green|first=Chloe Chaplain, Patrick|date=2018-05-05|title=The full list of results for London's local elections|url=https://www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/london-local-election-results-2018-the-full-list-of-outcomes-for-councils-across-the-capital-a3831926.html|access-date=2021-10-18|website=www.standard.co.uk|language=en}}</ref> The Harold Wood Residents Association, independent of the Havering Residents Association, formed a governing agreement with the Conservative Party on the night of the 2018 election.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Dailiy|first=The Havering|date=2021-01-28|title=Harold Wood Councillor's hit back at Havering Residents Association councillors.|url=https://thehaveringdaily.co.uk/2021/01/28/harold-wood-councillors-hit-back-at-havering-residents-association-councillors/|access-date=2021-10-16|website=The Havering Daily|language=en-GB}}</ref> The Conservative councillor Damian White, who had served as deputy leader of the council from 2014 to 2018, was made leader of the council following the election.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Coleman|first=Liam|date=2018-05-23|title=New Havering Council leader to be elected tonight|url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/new-havering-council-leader-to-be-elected-tonight-3168812|url-status=live|website=Romford Recorder|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210125103206/https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/new-havering-council-leader-to-be-elected-tonight-3168812 |archive-date=25 January 2021 }}</ref>

=== Council term ===

A residents' association councillor for Cranham ward, Clarence Barrett, died in March 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Anderson|first=Hayley|date=2019-03-14|title=Family of Councillor Clarence Barrett who died from a cardiac arrest raises money for public access defibrillators|url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/family-of-councillor-clarence-barrett-who-died-from-a-cardiac-3206910|access-date=2021-10-18|website=Romford Recorder|language=en-UK}}</ref> A by-election was held to fill his seat in May 2019, which was won by the residents' association candidate Linda van den Hende.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-05-18|title=New Cranham councillor to tackle parking and green space issues|url=https://www.time1075.net/148963-2-cranham-councillor-tackle-local-issue/|access-date=2021-10-18|website=Time 107.5 fm|language=en-GB}}</ref> In May 2019, a residents' association councillor for Elm Park, Sally Miller, defected to the Conservative Party.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Clemensen|first=Matthew|date=2019-05-14|title=Elm Park councillor defects from Residents' Group to join Havering Council's Conservative group|url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/elm-park-councillor-sally-miller-defects-to-havering-conservatives-3216586|url-status=live|website=Romford Recorder|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115151843/https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/elm-park-councillor-sally-miller-defects-to-havering-conservatives-3216586 |archive-date=15 January 2021 }}</ref>

Along with most other London boroughs, Havering was subject to a boundary review ahead of the 2022 election. The [[Local Government Boundary Commission for England]] (LGBCE) concluded that the council should have fifty-five councillors, an increase of one, and produced new election boundaries following a period of consultation.<ref name="RR">{{Cite web|last=Thomson|first=Charles|date=2021-05-13|title=Havering wards face axe as borough is split into 20 election areas|url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/havering-council-split-into-20-electoral-wards-7970006|access-date=2021-10-18|website=Romford Recorder|language=en-UK}}</ref> The Conservative councillor Bob Perry left his party after revealing he had secretly recorded a Conservative group meeting discussing ways to design election boundaries to be advantageous to them.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Cox|first=Michael|date=2021-04-07|title='He has to go': Ex-Tory councillor to take on council leader at next election|url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/bob-perry-to-stand-against-damian-white-7878568|url-status=live|website=Romford Recorder|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210407143657/https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/bob-perry-to-stand-against-damian-white-7878568 |archive-date=7 April 2021 }}</ref> In response, the LGBCE extended the period of consultation and made changes to planned ward boundaries.<ref name="RR" /> A three-member panel including two Conservative councillors and the independent councillor Linda Van der Hende was convened to decide whether to investigate the Conservative group leader, Damian White, over claims he had tried to [[Gerrymandering|gerrymander]] election boundaries for political gain. Reporters and the public were blocked from attending the meeting. The Conservative panel members voted to discard the complaints, against the advice of the council's director of law and governance, on the grounds that they were submitted more than ninety days after the recording had been made, even though they had been submitted shortly after the recording was published.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thomson |first=Charles |date=2020-10-16 |title=Conservatives dismiss expert's advice and throw out investigation into leader |url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/jon-cruddas-mp-blasts-damian-white-decision-6523808 |access-date=2022-03-23 |website=Romford Recorder |language=en-UK}}</ref>

== Campaign ==
[[Keith Prince]], the member of the [[London Assembly]] for the area, announced he was standing as a Conservative candidate in the council election.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Cox|first=Michael|date=2021-11-09|title=Assembly member Keith Prince reveals bid to become Havering councillor|url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/keith-prince-to-stand-as-havering-council-candidate-8475018|access-date=2022-02-15|website=Romford Recorder|language=en-UK}}</ref> Carol Perry announced she would stand for the [[Havering Residents Association]] in the same ward as the Conservative group leader who her husband Bob Perry had recorded saying that the council chief executive had let him affect the council's submission for new election boundaires so they would be "really politically advantageous".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gayne |first=Daniel |date=2022-03-01 |title=Havering leader faces election challenge by wife of Tory defector |url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/havering-leader-damian-white-faces-election-challenge-8723726 |access-date=2022-03-23 |website=Romford Recorder |language=en-UK}}</ref>

In March 2022, the council asked all staff to consider voluntary redundancy, aiming to remove 400 staff roles. The trade union [[Unison (trade union)|Unison]] and some councillors and local residents criticised the decision, saying that current staffing levels already meant long delays before getting a response from council staff, including one resident who waited three weeks for exposed asbestos to be removed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thomson |first=Charles |date=2022-03-10 |title=Havering Council invites all staff to request voluntary redundancy |url=https://www.romfordrecorder.co.uk/news/local-council/havering-council-voluntary-redundancy-scheme-for-all-staff-8746468 |access-date=2022-03-23 |website=Romford Recorder |language=en-UK}}</ref>

== Electoral process ==
Havering, as is the case for all London borough councils, elects all of its councillors at once every four years, with the previous election having taken place in 2018. The election took place by multi-member [[first-past-the-post voting]], with each ward being represented by two or three councillors. Electors had as many votes as there are councillors to be elected in their ward, with the top two or three being elected.

All [[Elections in the United Kingdom#Registration procedure|registered electors]] ([[British citizen|British]], [[Irish citizen|Irish]], [[Commonwealth citizen|Commonwealth]] and [[European Union]] citizens) living in London aged 18 or over were entitled to vote in the election. People who lived at two addresses in different councils, such as university students with different term-time and holiday addresses, were entitled to be registered for and vote in elections in both local authorities.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=How the elections work {{!}} London Councils|url=https://www.londoncouncils.gov.uk/who-runs-london/london-elections/how-elections-work|access-date=2021-09-14|website=www.londoncouncils.gov.uk}}</ref> Voting in-person at polling stations took place from 7:00 to 22:00 on election day, and voters were able to apply for postal votes or proxy votes in advance of the election.<ref name=":1" />
